name: PT SINAR TERANG MANDIRI Tbk

frontmatter.title: A nickel contract miner priced for liquidation after its largest client restarted
frontmatter.summary: MINE is a leveraged contract miner whose largest client halted for four months and has now restarted. The shares trade below book and near two times restated EBITDA, while our through-cycle cash-flow valuation is several times the market price. The gap is customer concentration and contract-renewal risk, not a broken business.
thesis: The FY2025 loss of profit was an accounting and mix effect, not a cash failure; operating cash flow exceeded net profit and the fleet build is complete.
Weda Bay Nickel, more than half of revenue, restarted in September 2026 after a four-month care-and-maintenance halt, removing the event the shares de-rated on.
A three-year contract with Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral and a new syndicated facility fund the next leg of volume without a rights issue.
The market price implies a permanent contraction in revenue; our base case implies Rp732 per share, a 234.8% total return.

The bear case is a contract loss at Weda Bay Nickel; the engine can only express it as a compounding growth cut, which still values the shares above today's price, but a true step loss would be worse and the bear is not a floor.

blocks.text: **BUY · target Rp732 · last Rp222 · total return 234.8%**

PT Sinar Terang Mandiri is not a nickel miner. It is a contract miner: it moves overburden, gets ore, hauls, barges and builds the roads and infrastructure its clients need, and is paid per cubic metre and per tonne rather than for the metal [S3]. That distinction drives everything in this report. MINE owns no reserve, sells no nickel and takes no direct price exposure; its economics are contract volumes, utilisation of a fleet of almost 1,000 units heavy-equipment units and the rates it negotiates with three clients who together supplied almost all of FY2025 revenue [S5][S12].

The shares have fallen from a twelve-month high of 515.0 to Rp222, a market capitalisation of IDR906.7bn against book equity of IDR934.9bn [S0][S5]. At that price the market pays 0.9x FY2026E book and 1.3x our FY2026E EBITDA measured at the model's FY2026E year-end net debt of IDR75.0bn [S0]. The trigger for the de-rating was visible: PT Weda Bay Nickel, which bought 1,252 IDR bn of MINE's 2,362.3 revenue in FY2025, suspended mining for four months and restarted only in September 2026 [S5][S9]. Our base case is that the restart holds, the ramp continues through 2027, and the three-year SCM contract and the new syndicated facility carry volumes while the Weda Bay relationship normalises.

The variant view is straightforward. The market is capitalising MINE as if the Weda Bay contract were lost permanently: at Rp222 our reverse DCF needs a -19.7% adjustment to our FY2027E revenue growth rate in every year of the plan — revenue shrinking, not growing. We think that is too pessimistic given a restart that Eramet has confirmed with government authorisation, even while conceding that Weda Bay itself cannot yet guide 2026 volumes [S9]. The risks are real and are concentrated in one relationship, one island and one financing; they are set out in section five. But the balance sheet is not broken (net debt IDR643.1bn, 1.0x FY2025 EBITDA), the fleet build that depressed 2025 margins is finished, and operating cash flow of 295 IDR bn already exceeded net profit of IDR202.0bn [S5].

Three things move the value: the Weda Bay volume path after the restart, the capex-to-depreciation gap that decides free cash flow, and the cost of the syndicated refinancing approved on 4 November 2026 [S7][S9]. Our target is Rp732, built from a DCF at a 12.5% WACC, cross-checked against the same eight years with no terminal value and against a P/E on the last audited year, and cut for illiquidity (section four).

MINE provides integrated mining services across five lines: mine planning and engineering; mine operations including land clearing, overburden removal, ore getting, grizzly work and stockpile management; integrated logistics including hauling, barging and transshipment; construction of roads, bridges, water management, reclamation and haul-road maintenance; and ancillary paving and stone-crushing [S3]. The company describes two decades of experience in Indonesian mining services [S3]. It operates almost 1,000 units heavy-equipment units and states that fleet capacity is the backbone of its operations [S12].

Revenue is highly concentrated by client and by site. In FY2025 PT Weda Bay Nickel accounted for 1,252 IDR bn of revenue, PT Hengjaya Mineralindo 629 IDR bn and PT Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral 348 IDR bn [S5]. Those three relationships are effectively the whole company. The active project list confirms the geography: Weda in North Maluku, Morowali in Central Sulawesi and Konawe in Southeast Sulawesi, plus a road-construction project for PT Erabaru Timur Lestari [S3]. MINE is therefore a challenger in a fragmented services market, not a price-setter: its position rests on equipment availability, mobilisation speed and relationships with the operators of three large nickel assets rather than on any resource it controls.

The growth engine since 2025 has been the Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral contract, won in May 2025. It covers mine-contractor services targeting 25.3 million bcm of production over three years and hauling of saprolite and gravel from Konawe to the Morowali industrial park targeting 13.5 million tonnes over the same period [S8]. Management flagged at signing that the contract required significant upfront investment and would weigh on short-term profitability — which is exactly what the FY2025 and 1H2026 depreciation lines show [S8]. SCM is a subsidiary of PT Merdeka Battery Materials, so the contract ties MINE to a second large nickel group alongside the Tsingshan-Eramet-Antam joint venture at Weda Bay [S8][S9].

The company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in March 2025. Net IPO proceeds were 130 IDR bn, of which about half was earmarked for heavy equipment and the balance largely for working capital, with a small amount used to buy land and buildings from the controlling shareholder [S12]. Control sits with PT Mitra Berkarya Sukses Selalu at 80.8% of shares, with 19.2% held by the public; the ultimate parent named in the related-party note is PT Stars Global Resources Indonesia [S10][S5]. The founding Sumendap family is represented on both the board and the shareholder register (section six).

The business model has one structural feature worth stating plainly: MINE is paid for work, not for metal. Contract rates are quoted per bcm moved or per tonne hauled, typically with indexed escalators, and the client bears the nickel price. That makes revenue more stable than a miner's but concentrates risk in contract continuity and client solvency — a trade-off that the Weda Bay Nickel receivable illustrates, peaking at 329 IDR bn at the 31 December 2025 balance-sheet date before collection took it to 162 IDR bn by 30 June 2026 [S4][S5].

Indonesian nickel is the demand engine of the global stainless and battery chain, and the policy lever is supply-side. The house metals deck carries nickel at US$17,500/t for FY2027E against a spot of US$16,324/t, with a long-run marker of US$17,500/t [S0]. For a contractor the nickel price matters only indirectly: it decides whether clients expand, idle or cut work plans. The more direct driver is permitting. The 2026 record shows how binding that is: Weda Bay Nickel halted for four months on an authorisation issue and restarted in September 2026, and Vale Indonesia also halted mining amid a delayed 2026 output approval [S9]. When the state slows work-plan approvals, contractors feel it first because they are paid by the volume their clients are allowed to move.

The demand side of the contractor market is the build-out of nickel processing capacity in Morowali and Weda Bay. Weda Bay Nickel is a joint venture of China's Tsingshan Holding Group as majority shareholder alongside Eramet and state-owned Antam; it was restarting progressively with contractor support, and Eramet warned that the pace depends on how quickly contractors and equipment can be remobilised, the yearly mining plan redesigned and administrative work completed [S9]. That sentence is the single most important industry fact for MINE: the client's own disclosure says the constraint on the ramp is contractor mobilisation, which is precisely what MINE sells.

Competition in contract mining is on fleet, safety record, mobilisation speed and price. The listed comparator set is the coal-mining contractors — Petrosea, Darma Henwa and Samindo Resources — because they share the paid-per-volume model, owned and leased fleets and similar client concentration [S0]. There is no listed pure nickel-mining-services peer in the archive, so peer multiples must be treated as indicative only. MINE's differentiation is narrow: integrated logistics (hauling, barging, transshipment) plus construction in one contractor is unusual for a mid-sized Indonesian firm, and the SCM award suggests the client set values that bundle [S3][S8]. Its weaknesses are equally clear: no proprietary technology, no resource ownership, and a customer base of three.

A contractor's revenue is only as durable as its clients' work plans, so the client mix deserves the same attention as the industry itself. In FY2025 Weda Bay Nickel bought 1,252 IDR bn of revenue and Hengjaya Mineralindo 629 IDR bn; the SCM contract, signed in May 2025, had contributed 348 IDR bn in its first partial year [S5]. Hengjaya is therefore the second client at roughly a quarter of the business on our arithmetic, and the archive discloses no term, volume or rate for it — a gap we flag rather than fill [S5][S12]. The SCM award is better documented: three years for 25.3 million bcm of mine-contractor production and 13.5 million tonnes of hauling, with management warning at signing that it required significant upfront investment and would weigh on near-term profit [S8]. Two things follow for the model. The SCM terms start to roll in 2028, which is why revenue growth slows after FY2027E, and the concentration risk here is contract terms and work-plan approvals rather than anything MINE controls. A nickel price at or above spot is the environment in which clients fund expansions and work plans, which is the channel through which a nickel tilt reaches a contractor's revenue.

Five forces, briefly. Buyer power is very high: three clients are effectively the market for MINE's services, and the largest is more than half of revenue [S5]. Supplier power is moderate to high on equipment — the prospectus names United Tractors and Sany among suppliers — and fuel is bought at market [S12][S5]. New entrants face capital barriers in fleet ownership but not technology barriers, so the threat is real at the margin. Substitutes are limited: miners either self-perform or contract, and the trend in Indonesian nickel has been toward contracting. Rivalry is intense and cyclical, priced per bcm.

Contract mining is a scale business with thin margins and high operating leverage. The global archetype is that contractors earn mid-single-digit margins through the cycle, expand when clients build and are the first to be squeezed when work plans are cut, because their fleets are financed with debt and leases. Indonesian nickel contractors have historically been tied to the industrial parks at Morowali and Weda Bay, and their fortunes have tracked the permitting cycle rather than the metal price itself.

The moat assessment is therefore weak-to-moderate. MINE has relationships and equipment, which are real but replicable; it has no reserve, no pricing power and no long-term take-or-pay contract disclosed. The method card's cost-curve test cannot be applied properly because MINE does not disclose a cash cost per bcm, so we cannot place it in a global cost quartile — a genuine gap in the evidence that we flag rather than fill (section four) [S12]. What can be said is that its clients sit on some of the lowest-cost nickel ore in the world, which is a source of volume durability even if it is not MINE's own cost position [S3][S5][S9].

Macro adds a second layer. The house macro deck carries the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD for FY2027E against a spot of Rp18,039/USD, and Brent at US$84.0/bbl for FY2027E after US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E [S0]. A weaker rupiah helps MINE's cost competitiveness against imported equipment and parts but raises the rupiah cost of dollar-denominated purchases; diesel is the largest single input, at 501 IDR bn of cost of revenues in FY2025 [S5]. The deck's 2026 oil spike is a genuine margin headwind and is treated as such in our numbers.

Revenue grew from IDR1,433.5bn in FY2022 to IDR2,362.3bn in FY2025 [S0], with FY2025 growth of 11.5% on the first full year of the SCM contracts and higher activity at Weda Bay [S5][S8]. The profit record is less flattering. Gross margin fell from 26.3% in FY2024 to 17.2% in FY2025 and net profit fell to IDR202.0bn, a decline of -34.0% in earnings per share [S5]. The cause is visible in the accounts rather than inferred: depreciation charged to cost of revenues rose to 350 IDR bn in FY2025 from a much smaller base in FY2024 as the fleet expanded, and 1H2026 depreciation in cost of revenues alone was 242 IDR bn [S5][S4]. The company spent IDR283.2bn of cash on fixed assets in FY2025 and added a further tranche through leases, so the depreciation step is the accounting recognition of a fleet that is now in place rather than a deterioration in contract economics [S5].

One restatement matters for anyone reading the data pack. The reported depreciation of IDR349.8bn in the FY2025 financial statements is the charge in the fixed-asset note, not the small figure a cash-flow-derived pack implies; on that basis FY2025 EBITDA is IDR656.0bn, a margin of 27.8% [S5]. The same restatement applies to capex and to 1H2026 depreciation, and it is why our EBITDA line is far above the naive EBIT-plus-nothing calculation.

The 1H2026 interim is the anchor for the current year, and FY2026E is built as that half plus a forecast second half, not as an annual ratio applied to the reported half. Revenue was 1,221 IDR bn against IDR2,362.3bn for the whole of FY2025, with net profit of 101 IDR bn [S4]. Weda Bay was in care and maintenance for four months and restarted in September, so the second half carries its own hole and the fourth quarter the early recovery: we model FY2026E revenue of IDR2,409.6bn, only 2.0% growth, with the second half slightly below the first [S9]. FY2026E net profit of IDR152.0bn is above the 101 IDR bn already reported, so the year is not a loss in the making: the second half is the smaller one because it carries the whole-year interest charge on the December 2025 debt and a normal tax charge against the deferred-tax credit that flattered the first half, not because the gross margin collapses [S4].

The margin path is where a base-year error is easiest to make, so it is calibrated on the reported half year rather than on the deck. FY2025 gross margin was 17.2%, and in 1H2026 the reported margin fell by less than a percentage point against that level even though Brent ran from US$68.1/bbl in FY2025 to US$96.0/bbl in the FY2026 deck [S4][S5][S0]. The company gave back almost nothing on that move, which tells us the fuel escalation in its contract rates works: we recover four fifths of any fuel move through rates, and the fifth that is not recovered is what holds FY2026E gross margin at 16.3% — the level the half year actually printed — before it recovers to 19.5% as the deck's oil path declines and the fleet's depreciation ratio falls [S4][S0].

Costs are dominated by fuel, labour, repairs and project operations. Fuel was 501 IDR bn of FY2025 cost of revenues, ahead of labour and repairs [S5]. Opex is the line the interim moved: operating expenses ran at a higher share of revenue in 1H2026 than in FY2025 because the related-party management fee rose to a half-year charge several times the FY2025 figure, and we hold FY2026E opex near the 1H2026 ratio of 5.2% before it eases as revenue scales the fixed cost [S4][S5]. Section six sets out what that fee is and why it matters.

Working capital is the second swing factor. The Weda Bay Nickel receivable peaked at 329 IDR bn at the 31 December 2025 balance-sheet date against FY2025 revenue of IDR2,362.3bn, and was the subject of an exchange query; by 30 June 2026 collection had taken it to 162 IDR bn and the ratio roughly halved [S5][S4]. We model working capital at 18.0% of revenue, between the year-end peak and the mid-year trough, reflecting a business that bills monthly and is paid late by a concentrated customer base. Because the valuation starts from the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, the part of that release that had already happened is not counted a second time (section four).

Cash generation is the strongest part of the story. Operating cash flow of 295 IDR bn exceeded net profit in FY2025, and cash capex of IDR283.2bn was the peak of the fleet build [S5]. The 1H2026 cash capex of about a third of the FY2025 figure reflects a completed programme [S4]. On our numbers free cash flow to the firm is IDR687.7bn in FY2026E and IDR442.8bn in FY2027E, which is what funds both the dividend and the refinancing.

The balance sheet is levered but serviceable, and it has already deleveraged. Total debt at the end of FY2025 was IDR812.5bn, of which lease liabilities of about IDR200.1bn were current at that date within total lease obligations of IDR422.7bn, the largest component alongside bank loans and consumer financing [S5][S4]. By 30 June 2026 gross debt had fallen to IDR594.2bn: the short-term bank loan was cleared and lease principal of 99.4 IDR bn was paid in the half year [S4]. Net debt was IDR643.1bn at 31 December 2025, 1.0x FY2025 EBITDA; on our forecast it falls to IDR75.0bn by the FY2026E year-end, 0.1x that year's EBITDA, as the repayment and cash generation land. Finance cost was IDR66.3bn in FY2025, an average cost near our 9.4% pre-tax assumption, and FY2027E carries IDR56.2bn because the model charges opening debt and now opens FY2027E on the actual 30 June 2026 balance [S5][S4]. The 4 November 2026 shareholder meeting approved pledging assets worth more than half of net worth to secure a syndicated facility led by KB Indonesia and SMBC Indonesia, to fund heavy-equipment capex and refinance existing facilities [S7]. That is a refinancing event to monitor, not a solvency event: the maturity profile is short and the facility addresses it, at a price the archive does not disclose.

Capital allocation is conservative on the dividend and aggressive on the fleet. FY2024 profit was retained in full; the FY2025 profit paid a dividend of 60.2 IDR bn in 2026, a payout of 29.8% [S12][S4][S5]. We hold a 30.0% payout, giving DPS of Rp11 in FY2026E and a yield of 5.0%, rising to Rp16 in FY2027E.

Earnings quality, run through the house screens. The accruals picture is clean in the latest year: operating cash flow of 295 IDR bn exceeded net profit of IDR202.0bn by a wide margin, so there is no sign of earnings outrunning cash [S5]. The one divergence flag is receivables: the Weda Bay Nickel receivable reached 329 IDR bn at the December 2025 date against FY2025 revenue of IDR2,362.3bn, far ahead of revenue growth, and the company was queried on it; collection to 162 IDR bn by 30 June 2026 is the right resolution but confirms the collection risk inherent in a single large client [S5][S4].

Related parties need more care than a one-line dismissal. Purchases from PT Sulawesi Energi Nusantara were 290 IDR bn in FY2024 and 6.3 IDR bn in FY2025 on the audited note, and nil in 1H2026 [S5][S4]: an affiliate that supplied a material share of cost of revenues in FY2024 stopped supplying it almost entirely a year later, and the FY2024 gross margin that we do not repeat was earned with that relationship in place. One inconsistency is stated rather than smoothed: the 1H2026 interim's comparative column shows 140 IDR bn of purchases from the same supplier in 1H2025 [S4], which cannot be a component of an audited full-year total of 6.3 IDR bn; either the interim comparative rests on a different basis or the audited note nets a second-half reversal, and no note explains which. We therefore build no trend from the half-year comparison and do not use it in the model — we rely on the audited annual figures — and we flag the gap. That is an optics-class flag, not manipulation-class — it is disclosed, and the direction of the change (a related-party supplier disappearing) is the one that removes a channel for value leakage rather than creating one — but it means the FY2024 margin is not a clean comparator. The other flow is the management fee to the ultimate parent, PT Stars Global Resources Indonesia: 15.6 IDR bn in FY2025, none in FY2024, and 25.2 IDR bn in 1H2026 alone, a run-rate several times the FY2025 charge against roughly two-fifths of 1H2026 operating expenses [S5][S4]. No basis for the fee or its step-up is disclosed in the archived record. We treat it as a real recurring cost in the model and as the single related-party item to watch, because a fee that triples in a year without a disclosed formula is exactly the gravity channel the screen is designed to catch. No special notation, monitoring-board status or late filing appears in the archived record, and the FY2025 statements are the audited annual accounts [S5]. We treat the FY2025 margin decline as optics rather than manipulation: it is fully explained by disclosed depreciation and the changed supplier mix.

Our forecasts, in short: FY2026E has a second half that is flat to slightly below the first at Weda Bay, with the restart lifting the fourth quarter, so the year still earns net profit of IDR152.0bn; FY2027E is the first full year of the restarted client plus a ramping SCM contract, with revenue of IDR2,650.5bn, EBITDA of IDR819.1bn and net profit of IDR221.3bn; FY2028E to FY2030E grow more slowly as the three-year contract terms roll and the client base broadens, reaching revenue of IDR3,186.0bn and a return on equity of 19.9%, which rests on the Weda Bay restart and the SCM contract delivering their stated volumes [S5][S8][S9].

We value MINE on discounted free cash flow to the firm as the primary method, weighted 70.0%, with the same eight explicit years valued again with no terminal value at a 10.0% weight, and a P/E cross-check at 20.0%. The method set follows the industry card for mining contractors. MINE owns no reserve and has no depleting asset, so a life-of-mine NAV is not available; it is levered — IDR594.2bn of debt at 30 June 2026, more than half of it lease liabilities — and capex-heavy, so a multiple alone would ignore both the debt and the fleet replacement cycle [S4][S5]. EV/EBITDA is deliberately excluded rather than run at a silent zero weight: the three listed contractor peers print anywhere from barely above one times to almost forty times trough EBITDA, and the median near thirteen times applied to MINE's LTM EBITDA would value the equity at more than four times our DCF — a cyclical-denominator artefact, not a benchmark [S0].

The discount rate is built bottom-up and shown in the table line by line, and the printed inputs reconcile to the rate the DCF actually uses. The build is the risk-free rate less the Indonesia sovereign default spread, plus the levered beta applied to the mature-market equity risk premium plus the Indonesia country risk premium. The risk-free rate is 7.4%; the sovereign default spread of 1.6% is deducted from it, because the same country risk is already carried in the country risk premium that the beta scales and charging it in both terms would count it twice. The mature-market premium is 4.2% and the country risk premium 2.5%. With an unlevered beta of 1.00 and market debt-to-equity of 0.66, the levered beta is 1.51, giving a cost of equity of 15.9%. Pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4%, weights are 60.4% equity and 39.6% debt at a 22.0% tax rate, and the WACC is 12.5% — the rate used both in the DCF and in the twelve-month roll to the target. A reader who adds the country premium to the risk-free rate without that deduction gets a materially higher cost of equity and a lower value; that additive convention is not the one the house uses, and the table shows the deduction explicitly so the arithmetic can be checked.

The DCF is explicit for eight years and carries a terminal value at 3.0% nominal growth: nominal because it is applied to nominal cash flows discounted at a nominal WACC of 12.5%, and one point below the house default because a contractor with three-year contract terms and one client at more than half of revenue has no perpetual claim beyond Indonesian nickel-mining activity growth [S5]. The terminal value is 45.4% of the DCF value, which is exactly why we do not rest the whole valuation on it. The same eight years with the terminal value removed entirely are worth Rp445 per share, -50.4% against the primary method, and that is the figure we would defend to a reader who believes the perpetuity is worth nothing. Our DCF gives an equity value of Rp898 per share and an enterprise value of IDR4,073.4bn. The key driver is not a commodity price — MINE sells contract services — but the volume path, anchored to the company's stated three-year contract targets of 25.3 million bcm and 13.5 million tonnes and to the Weda Bay restart [S8][S9].

Two mechanical points about the date. The valuation is not stale: it starts from the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, counts the half-year stub of FY2026E cash flow the engine computes from that date, discounts to today and then rolls the blended value twelve months forward at the 15.9% cost of equity, so the target and the Rp222 price sit on the same forward basis. The other is a timing adjustment made in the bridge, and it is the one place where a mechanical gain had to be taken out rather than added. The DCF opens on 30 June 2026, when the Weda Bay Nickel receivable had already fallen from its FY2025 peak of 329 IDR bn to 162 IDR bn [S4][S5]. That release is inside the opening net debt, so counting the model's full-year working-capital release again in the FY2026 stub would count it twice: the stub would credit the whole peak-to-June move while the true second-half movement is a rebuild of the receivable back to the normal ratio. We remove the difference between the two as a single bridge item sourced to the interim report, so the first cash flow starts from the 30 June working capital and every later year is untouched [S4].

The P/E cross-check applies 5.7x, the median of the three listed contractor peers, to LTM net profit — which at this date is the audited FY2025 year of IDR202.0bn — giving Rp283 per share, -68.5% against the DCF. Two disclosures matter more than the number. First, the median is a single name: the same three peers span a low single digit to more than forty times, so the cross-check is a range, not a settled benchmark and not a floor [S0]. Second, the earnings year matters more than the multiple. On our FY2026E net profit of IDR152.0bn — the trough year that carries the Weda Bay halt — the same 5.7x lands close to today's Rp222 and below the DCF, which is precisely why a trough year is the wrong base for a cyclical and why the P/E takes only 20.0%. A reader who rejects the DCF entirely and capitalises LTM earnings at the peer median would still value the shares above the market price.

Blending the three methods at our weights gives Rp730 per share; rolling that forward twelve months at the cost of equity and probability-weighting the three scenarios gives Rp814, and applying a 10.0% illiquidity discount — justified by daily traded value of IDR0.8bn, a small fraction of market capitalisation — gives a target of Rp732, a 234.8% total return including the forward dividend [S0].

The reverse DCF is the heart of the argument. At Rp222 the market is applying a -19.7% adjustment to our FY2027E revenue growth rate — a permanently shrinking business, not the 10.0% we forecast — which is what it looks like when the largest customer is assumed lost. Given that Eramet has confirmed the restart and that the constraint on the ramp is contractor mobilisation, which is MINE's product, we do not think that is the most probable path [S9]. The relevant caution is that Weda Bay itself declined to guide 2026 volumes, so the ramp could be slower than our FY2027E assumption; the bear case handles that.

Two anchors from the commodity-cyclical method card, stated explicitly. First, through-cycle versus spot: the DCF uses the house nickel deck at US$17,500/t for FY2027E against spot of US$16,324/t; a spot-derived valuation would be marginally lower, not the source of our upside [S0]. Second, the dividend anchor: at a 30.0% payout the FY2026E yield is 5.0%, so the market is plainly not pricing MINE on dividend capacity — it is pricing liquidation. Our valuation is a cash-flow valuation, not a dividend-yield valuation, and we say so because the two imply very different things at this price.

**Customer concentration — likelihood high, impact severe.** Weda Bay Nickel supplied 1,252 IDR bn of FY2025 revenue, Hengjaya 629 IDR bn and SCM 348 IDR bn [S5]. The loss or non-renewal of the Weda Bay contract on equivalent terms would remove more than half of revenue and strand fleet capacity. This is the risk the market is pricing and the one that dominates the bear case. It is mitigated, not eliminated, by the September 2026 restart and by the SCM contract, which was sized to add a second large client [S8][S9].

**Contract volume and renewal — likelihood medium, impact high.** The SCM award is a three-year contract for 25.3 million bcm of production and 13.5 million tonnes of hauling [S8]. When those terms roll, rates reset; a contractor that has invested in dedicated fleet has limited bargaining power at renewal.

**Leverage and refinancing — likelihood medium, impact medium.** Total debt was IDR812.5bn at 31 December 2025 and IDR594.2bn at 30 June 2026 after a half year of repayment, most of it lease liabilities, and the group has approved pledging more than half of net worth for a syndicated facility that both refinances existing borrowings and funds equipment [S5][S4][S7]. The refinancing risk is direct: a repricing of the lease and bank book would hit equity value, and an asset pledge reduces recovery for unsecured claims. Net debt of IDR643.1bn at 31 December 2025 is 1.0x FY2025 EBITDA, falling to IDR75.0bn at the FY2026E year-end — 0.1x that year's EBITDA — comfortable unless EBITDA halves [S4][S5].

**Fuel and cost inflation — likelihood high, impact medium.** Fuel is 501 IDR bn of cost of revenues and the deck has Brent at US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E against US$68.1/bbl realised in FY2025 [S5][S0]. We assume four-fifths of the fuel movement is recovered through contract rates, calibrated on the 1H2026 margin against the deck's FY2025-to-FY2026E Brent step rather than assumed [S0][S4]; full pass-through would be upside, and no pass-through at all would be materially worse than our numbers.

**Currency — likelihood medium, impact low-to-medium.** Revenue is rupiah, but equipment, parts and some contractor inputs are dollar-linked; the deck has the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD for FY2027E against Rp18,039/USD spot [S0].

**Regulatory and permitting — likelihood medium, impact high.** The Weda Bay halt was an authorisation event, and Vale Indonesia also halted on a delayed 2026 work-plan approval [S9]. Contractors do not hold the licences, but they bear the volume consequence when clients cannot move.

**Governance and related parties — likelihood low, impact medium.** Control is concentrated at 80.8%, and the group pays a management fee to its ultimate parent that has grown several-fold in a year [S10][S5][S4]. The fee is small against revenue but large against a fixed opex base; the risk is that it grows with the company (section six).

**Liquidity — likelihood certain, impact on exit.** Daily traded value is IDR0.8bn and the public float is 19.2% by the September 2025 shareholder report, so a position cannot be exited quickly; our target already carries a 10.0% discount for this.

The scenarios run the same three drivers, asymmetric by design rather than mirrored, and deliberately not stacked in one direction. The bear case assumes the Weda Bay relationship is lost rather than paused: revenue growth is cut by fifteen percentage points a year, gross margin gives back five points on an under-utilised fleet, and working capital stays near the FY2025 peak ratio; it values the shares at Rp344, still above today's Rp222. The bull case adds six points of growth, four points of margin and releases working capital as the restarted client ramps faster and the new facility fills idle fleet, valuing the shares at Rp1,464. Probabilities are 50.0% base, 30.0% bear and 20.0% bull [S9]. One limitation is disclosed rather than hidden: the engine applies a shock across the whole series, so the bear cannot show a single-year break in more than half of revenue. It expresses the same relationship loss as a permanently lower growth path worth Rp299 of fundamental value against Rp730 in the base, compounding down to roughly the scale of the contract by the end of the explicit period. The gap to a step loss is real and should be named: a single-year loss of the Weda Bay revenue of 1,252 IDR bn would remove all of it from the FY2027E base in one move, which is worse than anything the engine can price, so Rp344 is not a floor for the downside and we do not present it as one. The difference between the fifteen-point cut and the six-point addition is the concentration itself, not a bias: Weda Bay is half the business and there is no contract of comparable size to win, while the bull is better utilisation of fleet the company already owns. What we do claim is narrower and testable: every modelled case sits above today's Rp222 because the market has priced a contract loss the company has not suffered, and the observed restart is the evidence against it.

Signposts that would change the view: a slower-than-assumed Weda Bay ramp in the Q3 2026 report; any sign that the SCM contract is not delivering its stated volumes; a refinancing at a materially higher rate; a second halt; or the loss of a second client. Conversely, confirmation of 2027 volumes at Weda Bay would move us toward the bull case, and so would a syndicated facility signed at a materially lower rate than the 9.4% we carry in the model — we have not taken that as upside because the archive discloses the facility's purpose and the asset pledge but not its pricing [S7].

Ownership and control are concentrated. PT Mitra Berkarya Sukses Selalu holds 80.8% of the shares, the public holds 19.2%, and the ultimate parent named in the related-party note is PT Stars Global Resources Indonesia [S10][S5]. The President Commissioner, Sinjo Jefry Sumendap, is a member of the founding family, and a fellow family member sits on the board of directors [S10][S7]. The free float is therefore small enough that index inclusion and liquidity are structural constraints, not temporary ones. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the archived shareholder reports; the pledge of company assets approved in November 2026 is a corporate guarantee for the syndicated facility, not a share pledge [S7][S10].

The board was reshuffled at the 4 November 2026 extraordinary meeting: Ivo Wangarry remains President Director and Ade Irawan and Arabella Engelita Sumendap continue as directors [S10][S5], and Holmes Siringoringo, previously Chief Financial Officer, was appointed a director [S7]. An independent commissioner, Hendra Susanto, sits on the board [S10]. The concentration of ownership and the family representation on both the board and the shareholder register mean minority holders depend on the controlling shareholder's discipline; we see no evidence of abuse in the archived record, but the structure is not a check on it.

Related-party dealings are disclosed, and what changed is their direction. The related-party cost flow ran through PT Sulawesi Energi Nusantara, which supplied 290 IDR bn of cost of revenues in FY2024 and 6.3 IDR bn in FY2025 on the audited note, before disappearing from the 1H2026 accounts [S5][S4] — it was a supplier relationship, not a revenue one. The interim's 1H2025 comparative of 140 IDR bn for the same supplier does not reconcile to the audited full-year figure, so we rely on the annual note and treat the half-year comparison as an evidence gap (section three). What replaced it is the fee flow: management fees to the ultimate parent were nil in FY2024, 15.6 IDR bn in FY2025 and 25.2 IDR bn in 1H2026 alone [S5][S4], a run-rate several times the FY2025 charge and roughly two-fifths of 1H2026 operating expenses, with no disclosed formula or basis. The IPO proceeds also included a purchase of land and buildings from the controlling shareholder [S12]. None of these is large enough to be a value leak today, and we carry the fee as a real recurring cost in the model; the flag is that it is new, it has grown several-fold against a fixed opex base, and it has no disclosed basis.

The dividend record is short. FY2024 profit was retained in full; the FY2025 profit supported a dividend of 60.2 IDR bn, a payout of 29.8% [S12][S4][S5]. We hold a 30.0% payout in our forecasts because it is the only observed policy, and we note that a single year is thin evidence for a dividend commitment.

On audit, the FY2025 financial statements are the audited annual accounts and carry the full notes we rely on, but the text extract we archived does not include the auditor's report page, so we cannot name the audit firm or quote the opinion — a gap we flag rather than fill [S5]. The FY2026 interim is unaudited, as is normal for Indonesian half-year reporting.

ESG exposures are those of contract mining. Safety is the first: the Weda Bay restart was explicitly conditioned on safety and on contractor remobilisation [S9]. Mine rehabilitation and water management are part of MINE's construction scope, so environmental obligations sit partly with the contractor [S3]. The fleet is diesel-heavy, which is both an emissions and a cost exposure, and no transition plan is disclosed in the archived record. Community and labour relations in Morowali and Weda Bay are a sector-wide risk we cannot quantify from the company's disclosure. We do not score MINE on ESG beyond these observations; the evidence base is too thin for a rating.

The near-term catalyst is the Q3 2026 interim report, due within weeks of this note. It will be the first disclosure that spans the Weda Bay restart and should show whether the fourth quarter is recovering as we assume [S4][S9]. We will watch revenue against our IDR2,409.6bn FY2026E, the Weda Bay receivable, and whether gross margin holds at the 16.3% we forecast.

The second catalyst is the syndicated facility. Shareholders approved the asset pledge on 4 November 2026; signing, pricing and drawdown will tell us the refinancing cost and whether the equipment programme proceeds on schedule [S7]. A facility priced near the existing 9.4% pre-tax cost of debt is neutral; a materially higher rate would trim the target.

The third is the FY2026 audited result and the dividend decision in the first quarter of 2027, which will show whether the 30.0% payout becomes a policy [S5]. Beyond that, the monthly shareholder reports and any IDX disclosure on the Weda Bay relationship are the highest-value monitoring items, because they would signal a contract change before it reaches the accounts [S10].

The KPIs we monitor between updates: quarterly revenue and gross margin; the Weda Bay Nickel receivable balance and days; fleet utilisation and capex versus depreciation; net debt and the lease maturity ladder; the Brent price against the deck; and any change in the top-three client concentration [S4][S5][S0]. A deterioration in any two of these together would move us toward the bear case.

bear.narrative: Weda Bay Nickel is not renewed from the 2026 contract year and the relationship is lost, not paused: the largest client stops paying, revenue is impaired every year of the plan (the engine applies the shock across the series, so the 15pp cut compounds to roughly the size of the relationship by the end of the explicit period rather than breaking in one year), the fleet is under-utilised so gross margin gives back 5pp, and the receivable that a lost client stops paying stays on the balance sheet at the FY2025 peak ratio. [S5][S9]

The upside shock is deliberately smaller than the downside because concentration is asymmetric by construction — one client is 53% of revenue and there is no single contract of equivalent size to win. [S0][S5][S8][S9]

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +2%: 1H2026 revenue was Rp1,220,513m against Rp1,150,042m in 1H2025, and the whole-year build is that half plus a second half that carries the Weda Bay Nickel halt: WBN, 53% of FY2025 revenue, was in care and maintenance for four months and restarted only in September 2026, so H2 runs below H1 and Q4 carries the early recovery — a broadly flat year, not the H1 run-rate [S4][S9]. FY2027E +10% is the first full year of restarted WBN, the SCM mine-contractor and hauling contracts ramping on their 25.3m bcm and 13.5m tonnes three-year targets, and the equipment capacity the 4 Nov 2026 syndicated facility finances [S7][S8]. FY2028-30 moderate to +8/+6/+5% as the three-year contract terms roll and the client base is broadened [S12]. No company revenue guidance exists in the archived record.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Reported gross margin (cost of revenues includes depreciation, so this is the LK margin, not a cash margin): FY2025A 17.18%, 1H2026 16.24%, FY2024A 26.33% [S5][S4]. This input is the margin at base-year (FY2025) input costs, so FY2026E is the 1H2026 actual restated for the fuel the rates did not recover: 16.24% plus the roughly 1.8pp that the unrecovered fifth of a 41% Brent rise cost it, i.e. 18.0%, which puts the modelled FY2026E margin back on the reported half year [S4][S0]. The step-down from FY2024 is the depreciation of the fleet that grew from 419bn to 609bn of gross additions across FY2024-25, plus mobilisation of the SCM contracts; the recovery to 20% by FY2030E is the mechanical effect of D&A falling from 20% to 15% of revenue as capex runs below depreciation, not a price-led margin expansion. The FY2024 26.3% is not repeated because it pre-dates the fleet step-up and the related-party supply relationship that ended in FY2025 [S5].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1 - share of COGS exposed to Brent
assumptions.basis: Fuel was Rp500,596m of Rp1,956,519m cost of revenues in FY2025 (25.6%), the largest single direct-cost line ahead of labour (Rp340,201m) and repairs (Rp313,590m) [S5]. Only the fuel line is treated as Brent-exposed; labour, repairs, project operations and equipment rental are not.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1 - pass-through to contract rates
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the 1H2026 actual, not assumed: Brent averaged 68.1 in FY2025 and the deck carries 96.0 in FY2026E, a 41% rise, yet 1H2026 gross margin was 16.24% against 17.18% in 1H2025 (gross profit 198,210m on revenue 1,220,513m versus 220,447m) — a 0.94pp give-back [S4][S5][S0]. With 26% of cost of revenues fuel-exposed, that outcome needs roughly nine-tenths of the fuel move recovered through rates; we use 80%, which reproduces the 1H2026 margin and leaves a fifth of any further fuel move in the P&L. No archived source quotes an escalation clause, but the reported half year is direct evidence of the effective pass-through [S5][S8].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 4.22% of revenue; 1H2026 5.13% (operating expenses Rp62,598m on revenue Rp1,220,513m) [S5][S4]. The driver is the related-party management fee to PT Stars Global Resources Indonesia, which ran at Rp25,200m in 1H2026 against Rp7,800m in 1H2025 — a run-rate near Rp50bn a year and roughly 40% of 1H2026 opex, where FY2025 carried Rp15,600m and FY2024 nothing [S4][S5]. FY2026E is held at the 1H2026 actual ratio because that fee is a current, recurring charge; it eases to 4.3% only as revenue scales the fixed cost, and the 4.2% FY2025 ratio is no longer reproducible with the fee in place.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK, not the data pack: FY2025 total fixed-asset depreciation was Rp349,841m (14.8% of revenue) against the pack figure of Rp8,771m, and 1H2026 was Rp242,396m in cost of revenues alone (19.9% of 1H revenue) [S5][S4]. FY2026E 20% is the 1H2026 run-rate annualised; the taper to 15% is the consequence of capex held below depreciation, which shrinks the depreciating base as a share of revenue.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash acquisition of fixed assets was Rp283,175m in FY2025 (12.0% of revenue) in the fleet-expansion year and Rp81,409m in 1H2026 (6.7%) as the build completed [S5][S4]. The Nov 2026 syndicated facility explicitly funds heavy-equipment capex and refinancing [S7], and the fleet must be replaced at roughly its depreciation rate (14.5-20% of revenue), so capex rises to 14.5% by FY2030E and is held there: a path below D&A would liquidate the asset base rather than earn cash flow. Lease-financed additions (Rp326,222m in FY2025) sit in net debt, not in this cash-capex line [S5].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 25.3% of revenue was inflated by the Rp328,888m Weda Bay Nickel receivable that IDX queried; 1H2026 fell to 13.7% after collection (receivable Rp162,219m) [S5][S4]. 18% is the central ratio between the two, consistent with a business that bills monthly and is paid late by a single large customer.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 profit paid out as the Rp14.75 dividend in May 2026: Rp60,245m on net profit of Rp202,029m, 29.8% [S4][S5]. FY2024 profit was retained in full (no dividend), so the payout policy is new and 30% is the observed first-year rate, held flat.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Held at 3.0%, one percentage point below the 4% house default: a contract miner with three-year contract terms and one customer at half of revenue has no perpetuity claim beyond Indonesian nickel-mining activity growth, and 3.0% is inside long-run nominal GDP [S5].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Three-year average effective rate is 20.6% (FY2023 33.0%, FY2024 22.3%, FY2025 6.7%); FY2025 and 1H2026 were cut to 6.7% and 9.0% by deferred-tax credits (Rp21.8bn in 1H2026) and a final-tax layer, which do not repeat in perpetuity, so the 20.6% average is held against a 22% statutory rate [S5][S4].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The rate is the engine cost-of-capital pre-tax cost of debt, the IDR risk-free rate of 7.45% plus the house corporate debt spread of 2.00%, i.e. 9.45% — printed as 9.4% in the report and used identically in the WACC — so prose, assumptions and model carry one number. It brackets the observed cost: finance cost was Rp66,262m in FY2025 on average debt of Rp673.9bn, an effective 9.8%, and Rp34,191m in 1H2026 [S5][S4].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income was Rp1,593m on opening cash of Rp97.8bn (1.6%) in FY2025 and Rp1,059m in 1H2026 on Rp169.3bn; 1.2% is the observed deposit yield [S5][S4].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the deleveraging already reported, not a forecast: total debt fell from Rp812,454m at 31 December 2025 (short-term bank loan 94,506 plus current and non-current bank loans, consumer finance and lease liabilities) to Rp594,194m at 30 June 2026, a Rp218,260m repayment carried through the cash-flow line so the model opens FY2027E on the actual 30 June debt rather than the stale December balance [S4]. Lease principal of Rp99,446m was paid in 1H2026 alone and the short-term bank loan was cleared. No new net bank borrowing is added after that: lease additions refinance themselves and the 4 Nov 2026 syndicated facility funds equipment capex already inside the capex line and refinances existing facilities rather than adding to them [S5][S7].

assumptions.label: Minorities share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minority interest appears on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet (minority_bs zero) and all subsidiaries are wholly owned [S4].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 4,084,435,300 shares issued and fully paid at 31 December 2025; no rights issue, bonus or treasury operation is disclosed in the archived record [S5].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Held at zero: FY2025 other items were a Rp22,435m loss on asset disposal and a Rp2,269m FX loss, and 1H2026 had a Rp1,929m disposal gain; these are non-recurring and are not forecast [S5][S4].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E net profit is 85.1bn but 1H2026 already reported 101.1bn (S4), so the model implies an H2 2026 loss of -16.0bn. On the model lines, FY2026E gross profit 298.0 less the 1H2026 actual 198.2 leaves H2 at 8.4% gross margin versus 16.24% in 1H2026, on revenue only 2.6% lower. The only linked cost is Brent at 26% of COGS with 50% pass-through, which cannot produce a 7.8pp collapse; the 1H actual (margin -0.94pp while Brent rose) implies pass-through nearer 80%. A base-year calculation error, not a judgment.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The base year was double-counting the Brent spike on a margin input already calibrated to the post-spike half year. link1_pass is now 0.80 and gross_margin 18.0% at base-year input costs, so FY2026E reproduces the reported 1H2026 margin, net profit is 151.7 (above the 101.1 already reported) and no H2 loss is implied; H2 is built at the H2 deck and the Weda Bay ramp. [S4][S5][S0]

challenges.challenge: The section says the P/E is 5.7x our FY2026E earnings and explains the -67% gap to the DCF as a trough-year artefact. The model applies 5.73x to FY2025A net profit of 202.0bn (metric 202.029), not FY2026E 85.1bn; at 5.73x FY2026E the value is about Rp119, below the Rp222 price. The 5.73x is simply MYOH at 5.7x (PTRO 43.8x, DEWA 1.9x), so the peer median is one name.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The 5.73x is applied to LTM net profit, which at this date is the audited FY2025 year, not FY2026E, and section 4 now says so. It also discloses that the peer median is MYOH alone with the set spanning 43.8x to 1.9x, and that on our FY2026E net profit the same multiple lands close to today price and below the DCF, which is why the P/E carries 20%. [S0][S5]

challenges.challenge: 45% of the DCF value is terminal value at a 3% perpetuity for a business with three-year contract terms and one client at 53% of revenue. The text calls 3% real growth while the model applies it to nominal FCFF and a nominal 12.5% WACC, and no terminal-share or no-terminal-value sensitivity is shown.
challenges.answer: Accepted. 3.0% is nominal, applied to nominal FCFF against a nominal WACC, and the text no longer calls it real. A no-terminal-value DCF is now a third method at 10% weight (Rp445 per share, -50% vs the primary), the sensitivity grid covers terminal growth 2%-4% and WACC +/-1pp, and the terminal share of 45.4% is stated. [S5][S0]

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says Weda Bay is not renewed on equivalent terms, but the shocks are only -6pp revenue growth a year and -4pp gross margin. A 53% step revenue loss is never modelled, so the bear value of Rp497 (+124%) does not test the named risk and the 30% bear weight cannot be interpreted.
challenges.answer: Accepted as far as the engine allows. The bear now cuts revenue growth 15pp a year, gross margin 5pp and adds 7pp to working capital, valuing the shares at Rp344; the report states plainly that a single-year break in half of revenue cannot be expressed because shocks apply across the whole series and a percentage add is capped, so the contract loss is modelled as a permanently lower growth path that compounds to the size of the relationship. [S5][S9]

challenges.challenge: The report calls related-party flows small and cites FY2025 management fees of 15.6bn, but S4 shows 1H2026 management fees of 25.2bn against 7.8bn in 1H2025, about 40% of 1H2026 opex and annualising near 50bn. The 6.328bn figure is a related-party purchase, not revenue, and it fell from 289.993bn in FY2024 to 6.328bn in FY2025.
challenges.answer: Accepted and corrected. The 6.328bn is a purchase from PT Sulawesi Energi Nusantara, not revenue, and it fell from 289.993bn in FY2024 to nil in 1H2026; the management fee to the ultimate parent was 25.2bn in 1H2026 against 7.8bn in 1H2025, about two-fifths of opex and run-rating near 50bn. Both are restated as facts and reclassified under the gravity screen as optics-class, with the fee carried as a real recurring cost. [S5][S4]

challenges.challenge: The report states the Weda Bay Nickel receivable was 162bn at the FY2025 balance-sheet date. S4 shows 328.888bn at 31 December 2025 and 162.219bn at 30 June 2026, so the peak receivable is double the reported figure and 13.9% of FY2025 revenue.
challenges.answer: Accepted and corrected. The Weda Bay receivable was 328.888bn at 31 December 2025, 13.9% of FY2025 revenue, and 162.219bn at 30 June 2026. The report now dates the peak to the December balance-sheet date, ties it to the IDX query and to the collection-risk discussion, and the timing is handled in the valuation bridge. [S4][S5]

challenges.challenge: The revenue_growth basis cites S18, but the source registry holds S0 and S2-S12 and no S18 exists, while FY2026E revenue is a load-bearing input.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The S18 citation is removed and no unregistered source is cited anywhere in the report or the assumptions. FY2026E growth of 2% now rests on the 1H2026 actual in the interim report and the four-month Weda Bay care-and-maintenance period and September restart, with the FY2025 base from the audited accounts. [S4][S9][S5]

challenges.challenge: Several inputs sit below the latest actual without a source: NWC 18% of revenue versus 13.7% at 30 June 2026, FY2026E revenue growth +2% versus 1H2026 +6.1%, and interest on gross debt of 812.5bn from FY2025 versus 594.2bn at 30 June 2026, so FY2026E interest is 77.2bn against a 56.4bn run-rate. The capex justification also says long-run capex is 11% while capex_pct ends at 14.5%.
challenges.answer: Accepted. A net_borrowing of -218.26 aligns FY2027E opening debt to the 594.2bn at 30 June 2026 and FY2027E interest to 56.4bn; opex is held at the 1H2026 5.13%; working capital at 18% is the documented midpoint of the 25.3% peak and the 13.7% June ratio; and the capex justification now reads 14.5%, its terminal value, not 11%. [S4][S5][S7]

challenges.challenge: Hengjaya Mineralindo supplied 629bn, 27% of FY2025 revenue, and the SCM contract 348bn, but neither gets any volume, term or rate analysis. The bull case only re-rates Weda Bay and ignores the house FAVOR tilt on nickel and ID supply discipline.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 2 now sizes Hengjaya at 629.2bn and SCM at 347.6bn, states SCM three-year terms of 25.3m bcm and 13.5m tonnes rolling in 2028, flags that neither term nor rate is disclosed for Hengjaya, and puts the house FAVOR nickel tilt and the second-client ramp into the bull case alongside the Weda Bay restart. [S5][S8][S0]

challenges.challenge: The 4 November syndicated facility is assumed to cost the existing 9.5% with no new debt, and the just-completed 1,000-unit fleet's spare capacity at high incremental margin is not in any scenario.
challenges.answer: Accepted on spare fleet: utilisation of the completed fleet is in the bull narrative and its 4pp margin shock. The 100-150bp refinancing saving is rebutted with evidence: the archived EGMS coverage discloses the facility purpose, the asset pledge and the lenders but not its pricing, so a lower coupon would be an unsourced assumption; the 9.5% carried is the observed FY2025 and 1H2026 cost. A cheaper facility is named as an upside signpost. [S7][S5][S4]

challenges.challenge: The DCF is valued at 30 June 2026 (first cash-flow fraction 0.504, bridge net debt 217.7) but the blend is rolled one year at COE and compared with a 6 November 2026 price, so the roll date is undefined and about four months short. The half of FY2026E FCFF counted as H2 also includes 81bn of the full-year working-capital release that already occurred in 1H2026 and is in the 30 June net debt.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The report now states the valuation date: it starts from the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, discounts to today, and rolls twelve months at the cost of equity so target and price share a forward basis. A single bridge item removes the FY2026 working-capital release already inside the 30 June net debt, so the first cash flow starts from the 30 June working capital. [S4]

challenges.challenge: The peer set is three coal contractors because no nickel-services name is covered. The report concedes the multiple is indicative but still gives the resulting P/E 30% of the target, so a coal-contractor multiple sets a nickel contractor's floor.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The P/E weight is cut from 30% to 20% and a no-terminal-value DCF takes 10%, so a coal-contractor multiple no longer sets a floor; the report states that the median is one name spanning 43.8x to 1.9x and that on FY2026E earnings the multiple value sits near the market price, below the DCF. [S0][S5]

challenges.challenge: Section 5 prints 'a materially lower rate than the 0.1 we carry in the model' because {{in.cost_of_debt}} has no |pct filter: the client-facing report states a 0.1% cost of debt against the 9.4% pre-tax cost in the section 4 WACC build and the 9.45% actually used, a ~94x error in the one signpost covering a stated value driver (refinancing cost).
challenges.answer: The section 5 refinancing signpost now renders {{in.cost_of_debt|pct}}, so it prints the 9.45% the model uses and matches the 9.4% pre-tax cost of debt in the section 4 WACC table; no model or valuation number changed [S7].
